content: Crown ethers are heterocyclic chemical compounds that are cyclic oligomers of ethylene oxide in their simplest form. The fundamental repeating unit in any simple crown ether is the ethyleneoxy group (-CH2CH2O-). For example, this unit repeats twice in dioxane and six times in 18-crown-6. Macrocycles of the type (-CH2CH2O-)n, where n is 4 or greater, are generally referred to as crown ethers rather than their more complex systematic names. For instance, the systematic name of 18-crown-6 is 1,4,7,10,13,16-hexaoxacyclooctadecane. The term crown is derived from the structural resemblance of a crown ether bound to a cation, which looks like a crown sitting on a head. The first number in the name of a crown ether indicates the total number of atoms in the ring, while the second number specifies how many of those atoms are oxygen. Crown ethers are particularly notable for their ability to strongly solvate cations. This means that the equilibrium of the interaction is heavily shifted toward the formation of a complex between the crown ether and the cation. The oxygen atoms in the crown ether are ideally positioned to coordinate with a cation located in the interior of the ring, while the exterior of the ring is hydrophobic. This structural arrangement allows the complexed cation to dissolve in nonpolar solvents. The size of the crown ether's internal cavity determines the size of the cation it can effectively solvate. For example, 18-crown-6 has a high affinity for potassium ions, 15-crown-5 for sodium ions, and 12-crown-4 for lithium ions. The strong affinity of 18-crown-6 for potassium ions is one of the reasons for its toxicity in humans. Crown ethers are not the only macrocyclic ligands with a preference for potassium ions. Ionophores such as nonactin and valinomycin also exhibit a strong selectivity for potassium ions over other cations. Early research on crown ethers primarily focused on their synthetic production methods. It was only later that their unique properties and theoretical implications were fully appreciated. In 1967, Charles Pedersen, a chemist at DuPont, discovered a straightforward method for synthesizing a crown ether while attempting to create a complexing agent for divalent cations. His approach involved linking two catechol molecules through one hydroxyl group on each molecule. This would produce a compound capable of partially enveloping a cation and neutralizing the bound dication through ionization of the phenolic hydroxyl groups. However, Pedersen unexpectedly isolated a by-product that could bind potassium ions but lacked ionizable hydroxyl groups. Drawing on earlier research regarding the dissolution of potassium in 16-crown-4, he recognized that these cyclic polyethers represented a new class of complexing agents capable of binding alkali metal cations. Pedersen subsequently published a series of seminal papers detailing the synthesis and binding properties of crown ethers. His discovery had a profound impact on fields such as anionic synthetic reagents, phase transfer catalysis, and biological ion transport. For his groundbreaking work, Pedersen was awarded the 1987 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. In addition to its strong affinity for potassium ions, 18-crown-6 can also bind to protonated amines, forming highly stable complexes in both solution and the gas phase. Certain amino acids, such as lysine, have primary amine groups on their side chains. These protonated amino groups can interact with the cavity of 18-crown-6, forming stable complexes in the gas phase. The stability of these complexes is due to hydrogen bonds formed between the three hydrogen atoms of the protonated amine and three oxygen atoms of 18-crown-6. These hydrogen bonds contribute significantly to the stability of the resulting adduct. There are also aza-analogues of crown ethers, such as cyclen, which incorporate nitrogen atoms into the macrocyclic structure.
